title: Refinery margins watch
dek: Crack spreads, utilization, and turnarounds: how refinery economics set the bid for discounted heavy barrels like Western Canadian Select (WCS).

claims.text: A crack spread measures the difference between the purchase price of crude oil and the selling price of finished products, such as gasoline and distillate fuel, that a refinery produces from the crude. It is an indicator of the short-term profit margin of refineries, but it excludes other variable costs and all fixed costs.
claims.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

claims.text: The 3-2-1 spread approximates the product yield at a typical US refinery: for every three barrels of crude oil processed, the refinery makes two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillate fuel.
claims.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

claims.text: The calculation: add the spot price for two barrels of gasoline to one barrel of diesel (multiplying per-gallon quotes by 42 gallons per barrel), subtract the price of three barrels of crude, and divide by three to get a spread in dollars per barrel.
claims.source: US Energy Information Administration (EIA), crack spread explainer

claims.text: The 3-2-1 crack spread is the most widely used benchmark for US refiner profitability. It is traded on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), where refiners use it as a hedging instrument to lock in their margins.

The US 3-2-1 crack spread averaged $41.71 a barrel in the week to Nov 6, 2026, and stood at $36.86 a barrel on Nov 10, in calculations from US Energy Information Administration (EIA) spot prices published by Global Oil Shock. The diesel crack held near $98 a barrel in the week to Nov 6 while the gasoline crack eased to $13.57 a barrel, leaving distillate as the strong leg of the barrel, Global Oil Shock said.
claims.vintage: Data: week to Nov 6, 2026 and Nov 10, 2026; accessed 2026-11-16
claims.source: Global Oil Shock (EIA spot prices composite)

claims.text: The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its November report, published Nov 13, that global refinery throughput fell by 1.3 million barrels per day (b/d) in October to 81.3 million b/d, a seasonal low, and that it expects runs to recover to 84.7 million b/d in December. The agency also said persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off diesel supplies to international markets, keeping product cracks elevated even as crude supply moves into surplus.
claims.source: Declassified (reporting IEA November Oil Market Report)

claims.text: The US 3-2-1 crack spread stood at $39.32 a barrel on Nov 3, 2026, in the Eco3min composite built from US Energy Information Administration (EIA) spot prices for West Texas Intermediate at Cushing, New York Harbor conventional gasoline and New York Harbor No. 2 heating oil. The reading sits at the 96.7th percentile of the daily history since June 1986, against a historical average of $12.46 a barrel, and below the record of $78.92 a barrel set on Sep 25, 2026, Eco3min said.
claims.vintage: Data: Nov 3, 2026; dataset updated Nov 3, 2026; accessed 2026-11-10

claims.text: Reuters reported on Nov 5 that Asian refining margins cooled from their September records: Asian refiners' profit for gasoline slumped to its lowest since late February, while margins for 10 parts per million sulphur diesel were slightly above $60 a barrel, down from a record high of more than $87 a barrel in mid-September, LSEG data showed. Asian refiners are unlikely to increase crude purchases unless refining margins improve, a market participant told Reuters.

Gibson Energy said on its third-quarter 2026 earnings call on Nov 3 that its marketing business delivered $35 million of adjusted EBITDA, up from $7 million a year earlier, driven primarily by exceptionally strong refining margins at its Moose Jaw facility, and that it had hedged some of its distillate exposure into 2027 to lock in part of those profits. Consolidated adjusted EBITDA was a record $193 million and distributable cash flow was $120 million, the company said.
claims.source: Gibson Energy (Q3 2026 earnings call, via Roic AI transcript)

claims.text: OilPrice.com reported on Nov 5 that US refineries produced a smaller share of gasoline from every barrel processed in 2026 and shifted output toward diesel and jet fuel, citing Energy Information Administration (EIA) Petroleum Supply Monthly data through August published that day. Gasoline yields averaged below 45 percent from January through August, below the previous five-year low in every month, while distillate fuel oil yields exceeded their five-year average in every month, and jet fuel's share of output exceeded 12 percent in March for the first time on record and stayed at or above that level through August, the EIA said. The agency attributed the shift to particularly high refinery margins for distillate fuel oil and jet fuel.

Marathon Petroleum reported third-quarter 2026 results on Nov 3 with a Refining and Marketing margin of $45.70 a barrel, up from $17.60 a barrel in the third quarter of 2025, and crude capacity utilization of 100 percent, for total throughput of 3.2 million barrels per day (b/d). Refining and Marketing segment adjusted EBITDA was $9.9 billion, against $1.8 billion a year earlier, and the company said results were driven primarily by higher market crack spreads in all regions. Refining operating costs were $5.60 a barrel, against $5.59 a barrel a year earlier.
claims.source: Marathon Petroleum (Q3 2026 results, via PR Newswire)

claims.text: Reuters columnist Clyde Russell wrote on Nov 2 that Singapore gasoil, the building block for diesel, ended Oct 30 at $168.62 a barrel, down from the record $199.89 of March 30 but still 84 percent above the $91.42 of February 27, before the war, while Singapore gasoline ended at $127.64, up 61 percent from its pre-war level. Asia's imports of light and middle distillates were 6.15 million barrels per day in October, still 10 percent below the pre-war average, Russell wrote, citing Kpler data.

Reuters reported on Oct 28 that Phillips 66 posted a record quarterly profit for the third quarter, with net income of $5.62 billion and adjusted earnings of $14.08 a share against an $11.73 analyst average, powered by refining margins on fuel supply disruptions from the Iran and Ukraine wars. Realized refining margin was $38 a barrel, up from $24.08 in the second quarter, with a record distillate yield of 41 percent; Reuters said peers Valero Energy and HF Sinclair also posted record third-quarter profits.

Reuters reported on Oct 29 that northwest European gasoline refining margins fell by more than $3 a barrel on the day to hover near their lowest level since March, as gasoline stocks rose in both Europe and Singapore. The move marks cooling at the gasoline end of the barrel even while diesel and gasoil prices stay far above pre-war levels.

Sky Quarry, in a GlobeNewswire release carried Oct 23, calculated that Salt Lake City diesel rack prices indicated a crack spread of about $133 to $136 a barrel on Oct 21, 2026, compared with about $33 a barrel in January 2026. The release noted the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) expects low distillate inventories to keep diesel crack spreads elevated through 2027.

Northwest European refining margins collapsed in early October under the weight of crude acquisition and shipping costs: in north-west Europe, the crack spread fell from $54 a barrel at the start of September to as low as minus $11 a barrel earlier this month, LSEG data cited by The Guardian showed on Oct 14. The International Energy Agency said many refiners are shouldering the crippling cost of crude and fast-rising supertanker hire while making products such as naphtha and gasoline whose prices sit well below the highs seen for diesel and jet fuel. The Guardian noted the squeeze cuts the other way for refiners able to flex output toward diesel and jet: BP raised jet fuel production 30 percent in May and has since adjusted runs back to maximise diesel.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its October Oil Market Report that global diesel supply constraints are expected to persist into 2027, Bernama reported on Oct 15, citing Xinhua. Global diesel exports fell by 700,000 barrels per day year on year in September, as prolonged supply disruptions from escalating attacks on energy infrastructure in West Asia led to counter-seasonal stock draws ahead of autumn refinery maintenance and peak winter demand. Global diesel prices have eased from record highs of over $200 a barrel in September, but benchmark prices are still nearly twice as high as crude oil prices and almost double their pre-crisis levels, the agency said.

Forbes columnist Robert Rapier's third-quarter review found refiners leading energy stocks: Marathon Petroleum returned 55.1 percent in the quarter, Phillips 66 gained 51.8 percent, and Valero returned 49.4 percent, with smaller independents PBF Energy up nearly 70 percent and CVR Energy up almost 86 percent. Rapier argues refining capacity, not crude availability, has increasingly become the constraint, as disruptions to Russian and Middle Eastern refining capacity widened crack spreads. He cautions that refining is notoriously cyclical and unusually high margins can disappear as disrupted capacity returns.

CNBC reported Goldman Sachs expects global diesel and jet-fuel crack spreads to average above $40 a barrel in 2027, more than twice their usual level of around $20, even as the bank expects Brent crude to stabilize near $80 a barrel as Hormuz flows normalize. The bank's Nikhil Bhandari said product prices must stay high enough to keep some demand destruction going into next year, warning that any 2027 demand rebound would push the global refining system to its highest utilization in two decades. CLSA's Baden Moore added that underlying product demand remains intact and that rebuilding inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years.

Reuters reported the IEA's governing board is expected to decide the details of the G7's 100-million-barrel diesel and crude emergency release at an October 14-15 board meeting, after the October 3 G7 announcement gave no breakdown of crude versus diesel volumes, no participating countries, and no timeline. Italy would take part, one source said, and the EU's oil coordination group was set to meet October 7. The article notes the Iran war already triggered the biggest emergency release on record, 400 million barrels, in March, also coordinated by the IEA, and that oil prices fell more than $2 on October 6 as rising Middle Eastern exports and the G7 release eased supply concerns.

The EIA's third-quarter wrap put US refineries at unseasonally high levels in 3Q26, with utilization averaging 95 percent and plants processing the most crude oil for a third quarter since 2019, when refining capacity was 4 percent higher. The agency reported the quarterly average gasoline crack spread more than doubled its year-ago level despite fading in the second half of the quarter, while the distillate and jet-fuel crack spreads almost tripled theirs on tight global supply. In the week ending September 25, US distillate inventories sat 13 percent below their five-year average, gasoline 7 percent below, and jet fuel 3 percent above.

RBN Energy's daily 3-2-1 crack print stood at $64.65 a barrel on Oct 4, down $2.74 on the day, continuing the cool-off from the $73.12 near-record reading of Sep 22 and the $68.19 print of Sep 27 already on record.

China removed a swing supplier from the product market: Beijing did not authorize October fuel exports beyond Hong Kong and Macau, and state major PetroChina canceled some gasoline and jet cargoes already committed, per Reuters sources reported by OilPrice.com on Oct 1. Chinese refiners had exported 6.01 million tons of products in August, up 12.7 percent year on year, before the curbs; with domestic gasoline and diesel inventories at multi-year lows, refiners are prioritizing the home market.

The diesel-margin turn is dated: the ICE gasoil crack fell to about $70 a barrel on Oct 5 from as high as $85 in the middle of last week, after the G7 announced a release of up to 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency stocks over the next four months and the risk of a US diesel export ban receded, according to ING head of commodities strategy Warren Patterson. Patterson said the release only brings short-term relief, with diesel margins still historically high because the underlying middle-distillate tightness is unresolved.

The Trading Economics Crack Spread index, which tracks the spread between crude oil and refined products at the average US refinery, surged to a record 75 dollars a barrel in September 2026, up nearly 200 percent since mid-February. The report ties the spike to disrupted Middle East crude exports that pushed US refiners to run above 100 percent of nameplate capacity, and says the presidential administration weighed a ban on diesel exports as domestic gasoline and diesel prices climbed.

OilPrice.com reported on Nov 12, from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) weekly release for the week ended Nov 6, that US commercial crude inventories rose by 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million barrels, ending five straight weekly draws, while refinery crude runs rose by 322,000 barrels per day (b/d) to 17.0 million b/d and utilization rose to 95.2 percent. Gasoline inventories rose by 1.8 million barrels and distillate inventories rose by 4.1 million barrels to 103.3 million barrels, still 8 percent below the five-year average, and total commercial petroleum inventories rose by 11.4 million barrels, OilPrice.com said.
claims.vintage: EIA release Nov 12, 2026 (week ended Nov 6); accessed 2026-11-16

claims.text: OilPrice.com reported on Nov 4, from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) weekly release, that US crude inventories fell by 900,000 barrels in the week ended Oct 30 to 409.8 million barrels, 4 percent below the five-year average, while refinery crude runs rose by 199,000 barrels per day (b/d) to 16.7 million b/d and utilization rose 1.7 percentage points to 94.5 percent. Total commercial petroleum inventories slipped by 8.2 million barrels in the week, gasoline inventories fell by 200,000 barrels, and the four-week average for total products supplied rose to 21.2 million b/d, up 4.2 percent year on year, with the distillate four-week average at 4.2 million b/d, up 8.7 percent, OilPrice.com said. Distillate stocks fell by 3.6 million barrels to 99.3 million barrels in the same EIA release, according to EIA data reported by ENGINE Online.
claims.vintage: EIA release Nov 4, 2026 (week ended Oct 30); accessed 2026-11-09
claims.source: OilPrice.com (reporting EIA data); ENGINE Online (reporting EIA data)

claims.text: Reuters reported on Oct 28 that US refinery crude runs fell by 123,000 barrels per day in the week ended Oct 23 and national utilization fell 0.6 percentage points to 92.8 percent, per EIA data. US gasoline stocks rose 3.9 million barrels to 209.2 million even as Midwest gasoline stockpiles hit record lows, and distillate stocks fell 1.5 million barrels to 102.8 million, about 10 percent below the five-year average.

US Energy Information Administration (EIA) weekly data released Oct 28 showed Midwest (PADD 2) refinery utilization at 88.1 percent for the week ending Oct 23, down from 90.2 percent the week before, with crude oil inputs of 3.77 million barrels per day, down from 3.86 million, against operable capacity of 4.28 million barrels per day.
claims.vintage: Week ending Oct 23, 2026; released Oct 28, 2026; accessed 2026-11-02

claims.text: Reuters reported on Oct 21, citing US Energy Information Administration (EIA) data for the week ended Oct 16, that US refinery crude runs rose by 34,000 barrels per day and refinery utilization fell by 0.1 percentage points to 93.4 percent. Crude inventories fell by 3.06 million barrels to 412.5 million barrels, gasoline stocks fell by 2.95 million barrels to 205.3 million, and distillate stocks rose by 1.68 million barrels to 104.3 million.
claims.vintage: Week ending Oct 16, 2026; published Oct 21, 2026; accessed 2026-10-26

claims.text: IndexBox reported on Oct 23, citing Platts, that Enbridge Mainline apportionment for November stands at 19 percent for light crude at Kerrobert and 7 percent for heavy crude at Kerrobert, with a further 16 percent heavy point at Superior, up from 8 percent for lights and 4 percent for heavies in October. Trans Mountain apportionment for October stands at 7 percent, and the system was 90 percent full in September.

Oil Sands Magazine's Sep 30 third-quarter wrap puts the WCS discount topping $20 a barrel in September, the widest since December 2023, and attributes the jump to the unplanned ExxonMobil Joliet outage and a planned maintenance turnaround at BP's 440,000 b/d Whiting refinery in Indiana, which it calls the largest buyer of Alberta's diluted bitumen.

The Western Canadian Select (WCS) discount to West Texas Intermediate (WTI) stood at 21 dollars a barrel on Sep 21, per Argus market reporting, an unusually wide differential for 2026. With Friday's WTI settlement at 92.44 dollars, implied WCS was 71.44 dollars a barrel, down about 7.09 dollars on the week. Goldman Sachs' fourth-quarter 2026 Brent target of 85 dollars a barrel translates to WCS near 59 dollars, roughly 12.44 dollars below the current implied level.
claims.source: Oil Authority (citing Argus and Goldman Sachs)

claims.text: Midwest refiners invested billions of dollars in coking units to turn Canadian heavy crude into gasoline and diesel. BP's 430,000 barrel-per-day Whiting, Indiana refinery can process up to 85% heavy crude, up from 20% before the upgrades. That conversion hardware is the structural bid under WCS.

The flip side: when Whiting shut down on a transformer failure in February 2024, the WCS discount to WTI widened from $18.10 to $19.00 per barrel on brokerage marks in a single session, on fears of lost heavy-crude demand. Midwest refinery demand is the marginal bid under the barrel.

The same mechanism showed up in September 2026: with Exxon's Joliet refinery offline after a power outage, US refiners processed less crude and Canadian crude imports fell the most week on week. When Midwest runs drop, Canadian barrels are the first to feel it.
claims.source: Tim Dallinger (EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report summary)

claims.text: Competing heavy barrels are getting cheaper at the margin: Vitol and Trafigura, the trading houses marketing Venezuelan crude under the US-controlled export regime, were bidding Brent minus $18 to $20 a barrel for Merey cargoes bound for the US and Europe in late September, seeking steeper discounts as record tanker rates squeezed their margins. The two houses together moved about 597,000 barrels a day in August, more than half of Venezuela's roughly 1.17 million b/d of exports. A discounted Merey offer competes directly with WCS for the same Gulf Coast coker slots.

The competing barrel is a true substitute: Merey 16 runs about 16 degrees API with 2.5 to 2.7 percent sulfur, against WCS at about 21 degrees API and 3.5 percent sulfur. Merey is heavier but slightly less sour; both are delayed-coker feeds, and Merey is the grade US Gulf Coast coking refineries were built to run.
claims.source: Oil & Gas Journal (Merey assay); FuelBridge Merey 16 datasheet, Paraguaná lab Apr 2025; Oil Sands Magazine (WCS spec)

claims.text: Russia is set to extend its ban on most diesel exports beyond the end of September as Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries continue, with an extension of a month or more under consideration, according to people familiar with the matter. The move is cross-verified: the Russian business daily Vedomosti reported on Sep 16 that the ban would run to October 31, citing delayed refinery maintenance and the need to rebuild winter fuel reserves, and Energy Intelligence reported on Sep 18 that an October extension was likely.

Imperial Oil scheduled full turnarounds at two Canadian refineries in 2026: the 197,000 barrel-per-day Strathcona refinery near Edmonton in Q2, and the 124,000 barrel-per-day Sarnia refinery in Q3 and Q4.
claims.source: Oil and Gas Journal (citing Imperial Oil 2026 guidance)
